name: Carnosine
route: Applied to the skin, or taken by mouth as a supplement
status: Cosmetic and dietary supplement ingredient; not an FDA-approved drug
mechanism: A two-amino-acid molecule found in muscle and brain that buffers acid, mops up reactive molecules and blocks glycation (sugar damage to proteins)

article.summary: Carnosine is a natural dipeptide used in skincare as an antioxidant and anti-glycation agent. Support comes mainly from lab and skin-sample studies, not trials of wrinkles in people.
article.takeaway: Carnosine is a two-amino-acid molecule (beta-alanine plus histidine) found in muscle and brain. In the lab it neutralizes reactive molecules, binds metals and helps protect proteins from glycation, the sugar-driven damage linked to skin aging.[^1] In donated human skin kept alive in culture, a carnosine cream lowered markers of glycation damage after a sugar-derived stressor was added,[^2] but no trial shows that it smooths wrinkles on living faces. Taken by mouth, carnosine is split by an enzyme in blood,[^1] so sports research has focused on beta-alanine, one of its building blocks.[^3]
glance: Cosmetic and supplement ingredient (not an FDA-approved drug)
Antioxidant and anti-glycation skincare; oral supplements
Creams and serums; capsules and powders
Lab work, skin-sample studies, trials in other conditions

blocks.text: Carnosine is made in the body and is especially concentrated in muscle. Its chemistry explains most of its proposed benefits: it buffers acid, binds metal ions, soaks up reactive oxygen species and can react with sugar-derived molecules before they attach to proteins.[^1] That last property matters in skin, where collagen cross-linked by sugars (advanced glycation end-products, or AGEs) becomes stiff and discolored.
An enzyme in blood called serum carnosinase splits carnosine into beta-alanine and histidine,[^1] which is one reason oral carnosine and carnosine applied to skin are different propositions.

rows: Human skin explants, carnosine face cream (2018)
After methylglyoxal exposure, the cream lowered two glycation markers (CML and pentosidine) in both epidermis and dermis[^2]
Small average gain in exercise capacity and performance (effect size 0.18) in 1,461 participants[^3]
Promising preclinical and clinical results in diabetes, eye disease, aging and neurological disorders, with far more work needed[^1]

blocks.text: None of these show that carnosine reduces wrinkles in people. Skin-explant data show a chemical effect in tissue, not a visible benefit.

In skincare, carnosine appears in serums and creams, sometimes alongside peptides such as [acetyl tetrapeptide-5](/peptides/acetyl-tetrapeptide-5). Carnosine capsules and powders are sold as dietary supplements, which are not reviewed by FDA for effectiveness before sale.

Skin products can cause irritation or allergy, usually from the formula as a whole. Large trials of long-term carnosine supplementation are lacking, and safety in pregnancy or alongside medicines has not been well studied.
Cosmetics do not need FDA approval before sale, and a product that claims to change how skin works can be treated as a drug.[^4]

Carnosine is a well-known natural molecule with sound chemistry for fighting glycation and oxidation, but its skin benefit in people is unproven. Its better-supported role is as a precursor, beta-alanine, in sports research rather than as an anti-aging ingredient.

evidence.label: Limited: lab and skin-sample data for skin use
evidence.text: For skin, the best data are ex vivo skin explants.[^2] Oral beta-alanine has a larger human trial base, but for exercise rather than skin.[^3]

faq.q: Is carnosine the same as beta-alanine?
faq.a: No. Beta-alanine is one of carnosine's two building blocks. Because blood enzymes break carnosine apart,[^1] sports research has mostly tested beta-alanine supplements.[^3]
There is no evidence of that. Lab tests show less glycation damage in skin samples,[^2] but visible wrinkle improvement in people has not been shown.
Yes. It was first identified in meat, where it is abundant.[^1] Whether dietary carnosine changes skin has not been tested in the studies cited here.
